title: Concrete for House Building: Pouring, Curing; Ready-Mix or Hand-Mixed?
desc: How ready-mixed and hand-mixed concrete differ, how to pour, compact and cure house concrete, and choosing cement with a conformity declaration (2026).
summary: A guide for homeowners to understand the process of pouring, compacting and curing concrete, and a comparison of ready-mixed concrete with site-mixed concrete.
body: Concrete makes up most of the structural volume of a house. With the same design, concrete done well or badly can mean a house that lasts for decades or one that cracks and leaks early. This article helps homeowners grasp the key points.

Ready-mixed concrete (commercial concrete): mixed at a plant to a mix design, delivered by truck mixer, and pumped up to the site. Advantages: uniform quality, fast and continuous pouring, few construction joints. It needs access for the truck mixer and pump truck and tight time planning.

Site-mixed concrete: mixed by a mixing machine or by hand. Flexible for small volumes and narrow alleys; but quality depends heavily on material proportions, the amount of water and the workers' skill.

The choice depends on volume, site conditions and design requirements. The concrete strength grade is specified by the engineer on the drawings; homeowners should not downgrade it themselves to reduce costs.
2. Input materials: cement, sand, stone, water

Portland cement and blended Portland cement belong to the group of medium-risk materials that must have a conformity declaration (Article 12 and Appendix III of Circular 41/2026/TT-BXD, effective from 1 July 2026). When buying, check the packaging, label, origin and conformity declaration information. Sand and stone must be clean, with no mud or trash mixed in; mixing water must be clean. See also Building materials must have conformity certification.
Pour only after the formwork and reinforcement have been accepted; wet timber formwork before pouring.
Do not add water to the concrete on your own; if it is hard to pour, ask the engineer or the mixing plant for a suitable solution.
Pour in the sequence the engineer instructs, avoiding pouring from too high, which causes segregation.
Compact thoroughly so the concrete fills the space without honeycombing; do not vibrate too long in one spot.
Limit construction joints; if a stop is unavoidable, stop only at a location the engineer permits and treat the joint before pouring resumes.

Concrete needs moisture to develop strength. After pouring, shield it from sun and rain and keep the surface moist (watering, covering with damp sacks, tarpaulin, etc.) for the period given in the technical instructions. Do not stack heavy materials or walk heavily on a newly poured slab. Do not remove formwork or props before the engineer permits it.
For ready-mixed concrete: check the delivery ticket of each truck (concrete grade, time leaving the plant), observe the slump, and take test samples as the design requires.
For site-mixed concrete: control the material proportions as the engineer instructs, and samples may be taken for testing.

Keep the acceptance minutes and test results. Under Clause 2, Article 22 of Decree 207/2026/ND-CP, acceptance of work is based on the drawings, technical instructions, regulations, standards and material test results.
